tip: दवाई खिलाई (davaaee khilaaee) is literally 'fed the medicine' – खिलाना (khilaanaa) means making someone eat, and Hindi often uses it for medicine, not just देना (give).
The ending -कर (-kar) means 'having done it': ढोल बजाकर (dhol bajaakar = having beaten the drum). One small ending does the work of English 'by ...ing'.
ख़रीदी (khareedee) ends in -ee because मछली (machhlee = fish) is feminine – with ne the verb matches the thing bought, not the buyer. Anil's own gender never touches it.
One respected man, plural verb: वे रिटायर हो गए (ve retire ho gaye = they retired) said of a single person. Respect turns he into they, and the verb agrees.
नाना-नानी (naanaa-naanee) means specifically your mother's parents – your father's are दादा-दादी (daadaa-daadee). Hindi has no plain 'grandparents'; the side always shows.
-ते हुए (-te hue) = 'while doing': नाव खेते हुए (naav khete hue = while rowing the boat). Two actions in one sentence, no word for 'while' needed.
You ask FROM someone: वेटर से बिल माँगा (vetar se bil maangaa = asked the bill from the waiter). माँगना (maangnaa = ask for) always takes se, never ko.
Hindi pairs its linking words: जिस किसान ने (jis kisaan ne = the farmer who) opens, उसकी (uskee = that one's) answers. English drops the second half – Hindi says both.
You don't 'like' things in Hindi – they come to your liking: पसंद आया (pasand aayaa = came to liking). The dosa does the arriving; you just receive it.
कराया (karaayaa) = got it done by someone else: रिचार्ज कराया (recharge karaayaa) – the shop recharged it, I arranged it. किया (kiyaa) would mean I did it myself.
भेज दिया (bhej diyaa) adds देना (denaa = give) to 'sent' – the give part marks the job fully done, aimed at someone else. A bare भेजा (bhejaa) feels unfinished.
के (ke) + a word builds two-part position words: के लिए (ke liye = for), as in मेहमानों के लिए (mehmaanon ke liye = for the guests). Learn each pair as one chunk.
वाला (vaalaa) turns any noun into 'the one with it': ऑटो वाले (auto vaale) = the auto guy. Think chai vaalaa, rickshaw vaalaa – it names people by what they run.
करवाओ (karvaao) = have it done by someone else: जाँच नियमित करवाओ (jaanch niyamit karvaao) = get the check-up done regularly. Doing it yourself would be करो (karo).
A number plus -ों makes 'all of them': चारों बच्चे (chaaron bachche) = all four children, दोनों (donon) = both. English needs the extra word 'all'.
वाला (vaalaa) turns a noun into 'the one with it': ऑटो वाले ने (auto vaale ne) = the auto guy did. Same trick everywhere – चाय वाला (chai vaalaa) = the tea seller.
No verb 'to need' – the needed thing is the subject: बक्सा चाहिए (baksaa chaahiye = a box is needed). The person who needs it takes को (ko).
छाता ले लो (chhaataa le lo): the extra लो (lo) marks doing it for yourself. दे दो (de do) would mark doing it for someone else. Hindi tags who benefits.
Hindi chains actions with -कर (kar = having done): बिछाकर बैठो (bichhaakar baitho) = having spread it, sit. English says 'lay it out AND sit' – Hindi drops the 'and'.
One little ना (naa) does all of English's tag questions: सब ठीक है ना? (sab theek hai naa?) covers 'isn't it', 'right?', 'aren't you' – no matching verb needed.
English -ing never changes, but रही (rahi) does: Shobha gets दौड़ रही है (daud rahi hai) because she's female – a man would be दौड़ रहा है (daud raha hai).
Phone Hindi skips 'this is' – you say who you are directly: मैं डॉक्टर शर्मा बोल रहा हूँ (main Doctor Sharma bol raha hoon = I am Doctor Sharma speaking).
One doctor, plural verb: respect turns देख रहा है (dekh raha hai) into देख रहे हैं (dekh rahe hain). Elders, doctors and bosses get the plural form even when they're one person.
उड़ाना (udaanaa) means 'make fly': kids are पतंग उड़ा रहे हैं (patang udaa rahe hain), making the kite fly. Plain उड़ना (udnaa) is what the kite itself does.
-इए is the respectful command: धीरे बोलिए (dheere boliye = please speak slowly). बोलो (bolo) is the plain version you'd use with friends.
मिलना (milnaa) means both 'meet' and 'get'. Here मिल रहे हैं (mil rahe hain) = we're meeting; but पानी मिल रहा है (paanee mil raha hai) would mean water is available.
For 'I have been studying', Hindi uses the present continuous plus से (se = since): तीन महीने से हिंदी पढ़ रहा हूँ (teen maheene se hindi parh raha hoon).
'Is sitting' is NOT बैठ रहे (baith rahe) – that means in the act of sitting down. The seated state uses बैठे (baithe): बैठे अख़बार पढ़ रहे हैं (baithe akhbaar parh rahe hain) = seated, reading.
Doubling जैसे-जैसे (jaise-jaise) means 'as... steadily': जैसे-जैसे शहर बढ़ रहा है (jaise-jaise shahar barh raha hai) = as the city keeps growing.
No dummy 'it' for weather – rain and drizzle just happen: बूँदा-बाँदी हो रही है (boondaa-baandee ho rahi hai = drizzle is happening).
